ow what a summer we are having. I hope you have been able to stay cool.
We often talk about how to minimize wood cracking, but hardly ever talk about
what to do with a cracked piece. I enjoyed the article in the AAW’s magazine
American Woodturner this month called ‘When Good Wood Cracks’. It’s about making a
cracked piece into a beautiful piece of art. Some great tips and suggestions.
Speaking of the AAW, eight of our members participated in an AAW sponsored focus group
to help them understand how they can better serve their members. Focus groups have been
held with guilds from all over the US and Canada. It will be interesting to see how the information to direct the services the AAW can and should provide for its members.
Art has lined up a wonderful group of turners for us this year. Betty Scarpino, Micheal Hosaluk, Steve Kennard, Kurt Hertzog and there may be some others in the works. We are fortunate to have this caliber of turner’s come and demo/teach for us. I hope you will take advantage of the opportunity.
Enjoy the rest of the summer and Happy Turning!
Bill
September’s President’s Challenge: A Cup and a Saucer

Editor's Notes
This is the first time we have published a summer newsletter. I have tried to capture some
of the things that did/are happening this Summer as well as look at the line-up for the new
year. We honoured one of our own in June by giving Don Hoskins’ our prestigious Outstanding Contribution Award. We included a reprinted the details of Don’s award for you
to review. Ed Pretty sent us an interesting article on “Wave Form” turnings that has been
keeping him busy. Both Anne Rostvig and Al Cusworth sent reports on summer demonstration that they hosted to promote the Guild. We look ahead to the 2015-16 season and
the exciting demonstrations that are coming up. And, we take a closer look at Dennis
Houle’s beautiful vessel from the June Instant Gallery.
We hope you enjoy this issue and that it gives you a rolling start to our next meeting on
September 23, 2015.

Front Cover:
17” tall slender vase
by Dennis Houle

Page 4
GVWG
Dennis Houle has been contributing beautiful pieces to the Instant gallery for some time so it is not
much of a surprise that he had another hit at the June meeting. This piece is a 17” tall slender vase
made from ambrosia maple with 9” walnut legs. I had a chance to talk to Dennis first about his piece and
then about what turning means for him.
Dennis said he spoke to Avelino Samuel when he was here (June 2011) about the wood he used and in
particular, the ambrosia maple. Avelino said he used an arborist in North Carolina named Elvie Jackson. By coincidence Dennis and his wife were planning a cross country driving holiday and he took an
80 mile side trip to look up Elvie and buy some ambrosia maple. The wood sat drying in his shop for
almost 4 years before he started the piece.
Dennis went on to say that his wife wanted a tall vase so he went to
the Internet to look up examples. He discussed several designs with
members of the club and refined his own shape from those talks.
One of the changes was the feet. The examples had shorter, heavier
feet and Dennis wanted something lighter but also something that
would lift the vessel higher. The resulting walnut feet were carefully
designed so both the inside and outside curves echo the curve of the
vessel and the positioning of the attachment points were at a
“pleasing” location. Finally, the flared lip of the vessel was because
his wife wanted it that way.
I asked Dennis about challenges he encountered and not surprisingly he said that hollowing that deep was very difficult. Once over
about 9” deep the chatter became significant even with his homemade ¾” hollowing bar and Berger cutter.
Once it was done, Dennis finished it with 9 or 10 coats of wipe-on poly power sanding at 1000 grit between coats and buff polishing it with 1500 for the last coat. The result was certainly with the effort.
Finally I asked Dennis how he got started turning and why he continues. He said on one of his Arizona
winter getaways he was in an RV park with a large wood shop and saw several people turning. They got
him on the lathe and he really enjoyed it. After returning to Vancouver, he took a class at Lee Valley
where the instructor suggested he join the Guild.
Dennis likes the challenge of turning and seeing what is hidden in the wood. He will go months without
turning and then get inspired and spend long hours turning. We are lucky to have him in the Guild so
we can see the results of his careful and thoughtful efforts.
Bruce Campbell
A Closer Look

Page 5
GVWG
I thought I would share a project I have been working on recently that is different than many and uses a
hollowing technique I haven’t used until now. The size of this project is a bit nuts but the concept may
be something that might come in handy no matter what the size.
Some of you may have seen my spiral pieces cut from tall vase forms. The one below is my favourite,
standing 22” tall. It now lives somewhere in the UK.
That form has morphed into several iterations, each one a spiral cut from a completed turning. In some
cases, I have been able to use the negative space cut from the original for yet another piece, so that’s a
cool bonus. Most of these pieces now go to a friend, Steve Smith, who is a native artist. Steve paints his
very contemporary style on these pieces, which are themselves anything but traditional native forms.
This has been a very rewarding collaboration for both of us. Quite honestly I feel that I gain the most,
Ed PreƩy
Something Different

Page 6
GVWG
having learned so much from him about art, inspiration and life in general.
For several years I have had an idea of a wave-like form in my mind, but no surface treatment to take it
to the next level. Recently it came out in its own time as something that would suit Steve’s style perfectly. He agreed with my ideas so I started the project immediately – by falling a large maple on Sumas
Mountain.
The piece needed to be at least 36” long by at least 8” in diameter (so that Steve could paint the inside).
Ideally the blank had to be centered with the pith in the middle to keep the dried piece from being oval.
The stems from the tree I chose were perfect. I had the length and got 9” and 10” diameter pieces. At the
moment the rest is taking up a lot of space beside my shop.
(Continued on page 7)

Page 7
GVWG
The plan was to make a 33” long “pipe” with ½” wall thickness then cut a wave form from that (to my
great satisfaction, I actually get two from each one). I started by turning a cylinder between centers. I
used a faceplate since this was a very heavy piece. To begin the hollowing I set up a steady rest then removed the tailstock. After boring out the center I used a large hollowing rig to hollow the piece to the
middle plus a bit.
I removed the piece from the lathe and faceplate then affixed a blank to the faceplate and turned it as a
“plug” for the hollow end. I glued the plug, complete with faceplate, into the piece using the lathe as a
clamp. Once set, I proceeded to hollow the second half. Parting the completed piece from the plug was a
bit of an adventure but everything went as planned with the steady rest and a giant taper center on the
tailstock end controlling things.

Page 8
GVWG
Mapping the spiral is the same technique used for marking out barley twists on spindles. I used the indexing head and divided the diameter into equal parts (24, I think) and marking the lines with the tool
rest set exactly at center. I then divided the length into equal parts by using a set of dividers to step off.
The trial and error method of making minute adjustments to the dividers to get to the exact destination
didn’t really take all that long and achieved the end result I wanted. By using a flexible ruler (courtesy of
Barry Wilkinson – Thanks, Barry) I was able to connect the dots (intersections) to get my cutting lines.
The ends of the wave were drawn free form to give it at least a bit of an organic look. We were even able
to use the waste pieces from the end of the waves for little shelf-mounted forms (See photo of pieces on
counter top. Pardon the laundry.)
(Continued on page 9)

Page 9
GVWG
After waiting for a few weeks for the piece to dry, it was a matter of cutting carefully on the lines and
sanding the pieces. And sanding. And sanding. And sanding some more. In the end, I did quite a bit of
sanding. Times four. A couple of small turned buttons on the bottom keep the wave from crashing on
the beach – or the floor.
At this point in time the work is in Steve’s hands and I have no idea what he will come up with. My original inspiration was under-sea creatures on the inside and over-the-sea-creatures on the outside. Time
will tell because he is very much an artist who works in the moment. There are four of these and it will
take a couple of months at least for him to paint.

On the second Saturday of each month, the Guild
sponsors a learning session known as Turning 101.
The focus of these sessions is to introduce new
turners to safe practices through simple projects
that can often be finished in a single session. The
Turning 101 Coordinator is Gerry Vickers who
picks the topics, arranges the instructor for each
session, registers the attendees, gathers the money,
arranges for the materials and then attends the
sessions to help out. A growing number of members of our Guild began their turning through
Turning 101.
All sessions run from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM on the
second Saturday of the month except for the December session which is on the first Saturday. All
sessions are held at the classroom facilities at KMS
Tools, 925 Tupperware Avenue, Coquitlam BC and
cost $25.00 per person per session. Please note
that there are only six spaces in each class assigned
on a first-paid basis and the sessions are restricted
to Guild members only. Unfortunately, Gerry cannot take membership payments at the door. You
must have attended at least one Guild meeting prior where you can join up.
Dates have been booked through 2016 and some
topics have been chosen but keep an eye on the
newsletter for details as they come available.

We are well into summer now and it may be a
little difficult to recall the excellent spoon
turning demonstration that Dennis Cloutier
gave at our last meeting.
He wanted to turn a spoon that was more like
those we all have at home rather than the more
common ball-on-a-stick (fig 5.1) type or the
flat board cutout type (fig 5.2). He wanted an
egg shaped bowl with the handle connecting at
the lip. To do this he reasoned he should start
with a blank that could be cut in two after the
initial turning and then use several multicenter axes to refine the shape.
fig 5.1
fig 5.2
He started with a square blank long enough to
include both bowl and handle plus a little and
turned it round between centers. Then he
turned an egg shape on one end and a post the
rest of the way.
fig 5.3
Note the wood left on each end - this is important in the next step. Then he band sawed
the blank in half.
fig 5.4
(Continued on page 12)
Bruce Campbell
Turning Cloutier‐style wooden spoons

Page 12
GVWG
We enjoyed some discussion about leaving
these end pieces square to make it easier to cut
the piece in half and we also talked about gluing two pieces of wood together with a sheet of
newspaper in between so they could be split
apart after. Certainly both would work.
Now on each end lay out two new centers as
shown in fig 5.5.
fig 5.5
Use that new center to mount the blank and
turn the handle to its final shape.
After the handle is done, Dennis cuts off the
end bits on the bandsaw and sands then
smooth. This leaves just the bowl to the finished. While a little refinement can be done
on the lathe, the majority of the work on the
bowl must be done off the lathe. Dennis first
refines the outside of the bowl with sanders
and power carvers to get it to the desired shape
and then uses a rotary tool with an aggressive
burr to rough out the inside. His comment is
that this goes surprisingly quickly with a proper selection of burrs.
Dennis discussed a number of additional possibilities with this approach:
The use of more centers to get the handle
offset relative to the bowl of the spoon;
Use offsets to turn the bottom of the bowl
to make it more shallow (this must be done
before the blank is cut in half);
but he left the details of how to do this for us to
work out.
Many thanks, Dennis for sharing your unique
project with us.
(Continued from page 11)

Page 13
GVWG
In 2007 our Board created the Outstanding Contribution Award as a way to recognize those members
that have done things for the Guild that made us a better organization. Our first recipient was Art
Liestman, our founding president and at our June meeting we gave the award to our second recipient,
founding member and our first treasurer, Don Hoskins. Here is the citation given at the meeting followed by remarks from our first recipient, Art.
Don Hoskins is a founding member of the GVWG and served as our first treasurer form 1999 to
2004. But his contributions began well before the Guild started. He was instrumental in getting the
GVWG registered as a friendly society in British Columbia and even put up seed money along with
the other founders to give the fledgling Guild some working capital.
Through his connections with Belcerra council he secured the Belcerra Community Hall for our first
demonstration and class with Bonnie Klein. He also used his council connections to get a place at
Port Moody Arts Centre for our Board to hold its regular meetings – a space we still use today.
While he has done some “up front” things for the Guild, he has also done a LOT behind the scenes.
He has hosted a number of our visiting demonstrators; served on our elections search committee; acted as the demonstrator liaison for all three of our regional symposia; and has always “been there” for
just about all Guild activities.
A number of us that have served as Board members used Don as a senior statesman where we could
explore problems and brain-storm solutions. Personally, I found his insight to be excellent and his
patience nearly inexhaustible.
Don also has a ready wit and delightful sense of humour. I can still remember his financial report
from one of our early AGM meetings:
“we started with some money; we brought in some money; we spent some money;
we have money left. Any questions?”
But perhaps Don’s most powerful contribution, one that impacts us all, but of which few of us are
aware, is his research and drafting of the letter of invitation we provide our foreign demonstrator.
That letter spells out the exact clause in Canadian Law that allows demonstrators to enter the country
and teach for a few days without a visa. Since Don developed that letter we have never had a problem getting international demonstrators into the country and that has been a huge benefit to us all.
As a turner Don has been known in the Tri-cities area for years. I remember seeing a display of his
work at Coquitlam Centre several years before the Guild was formed and he and Des Wilson have
been perennial demonstrators at IOCO Days for years – often in the pouring rain.
March 25
Don Hoskins given Outstanding
Contribution Award

Don is also a collector of wood art. A visit to his house is like visiting a woodturning gallery except
few galleries would have used a Richard Raffan bowl as a dog dish – but Don did.
So today the Board of the GVWG presents its highest award to
Mr. Donald Hoskins
and names him a life-time member of the Greater Vancouver Woodturners Guild.
From Art Liestman
I want to add my personal congratulations to my dear friend Don Hoskins on being honoured with a
well-deserved GVWG lifetime membership. Thank you, Don, for your years of service as an officer
in the guild and many more years of work behind the scenes in various roles, both formal and informal. I'd personally like to thank you for the countless times that you acted as sounding board and
advisor to me during my time as President and in more recent years in my role as demonstrator inviter. Congratulations, Don, and thank you for your long-time support and dedication to our guild.

On July 4th, a few members of the Guild took part in
Art in the Park Day at the Haney Farmers Market in
Maple Ridge.
It was our fifth year participating in this event which
brings together various local artist and artisan groups
to strut their stuff for the market visitors. Maple Ridge
is known for its artistic community and included in the
event were the local
painting group, the
weavers and spinners,
jewellers and furniture
makers as well as other
fascinating activities. It
was an extremely hot
day, but that didn't
affect the attendance
and business was brisk.
Gerry had the forethought to prepare some tops ahead
of time and these are always a hit with the children. In
fact, it is the children who seem to bring in their parents, who then stay to watch the demo and browse the
display tables.
As always, people are fascinated by the beauty
of the wood.
Many have no
idea that such
variety exists
and that there is
a way to bring it
out which is both satisfying and environmentally responsible. This market prides itself on its 'green' footprint and our display fit well into that role. Jean and I
talked ourselves hoarse, explaining the process, showing off our wares and promoting the Guild.
This is a very busy, vibrant market with a great atmosphere and it is always a pleasure to be part of it. It has
been operating for more than ten years now and has
grown from just 15 vendors in the beginning to a total
on that Saturday of 77. I became involved some years
ago as a board member and am happy to maintain that
association through this event. We handed out a great
many membership brochures
which we hope
will translate
into new members come September.
This year the
event was a
little later than
usual and some of our stalwarts were unavailable so we
restricted ourselves to only two lathes. However, we
didn't notice any lack of support from market visitors
and the event was a great success as usual. Thanks, as
always, go to Gerry Vickers who has been my willing
partner throughout, as well as to Dan Moleschi and
Keith and Jean Ruttan. Special thanks to Jean who
helped me out so much with the display. Thanks also to
Bill Fowle who came for a brief visit and ended up staying for most of the time fielding questions. Your efforts
were much appreciated.
Anne Rostvig
Maple Ridge Demo

Page 16
GVWG
By Allan Cusworth
Three Guild Members Demonstrate at Arts
Alive 2015 in Langley
On August 15,
2015, Jay Mapson, Phil Vetra
and Allan Cusworth set up
canopies in
Langley City at
the annual
Downtown
Langley Business Association’s Arts Alive
Festival. This is the fifth year that these and other
GVWG and FVWG turners have been demonstrating at Arts Alive. Each year the display gets bigger
and more successful. Allan’s wife Natalia, and Jay’s
wife, Lin filled the important role of sales and marketing specialists by attending to the sales table
while the turners demonstrated and visited with
the customers.
The weather cooperated by shedding the
rain clouds just before the 10:00 am
festival opening time.
The crowd was large,
and the interest in
woodturning was fantastic with a number
of people saying that
they turned at high school and were thinking of
trying to start the hobby again. We handed out a
number of guild meeting invitations.
As the pictures show,
we had a great time
demonstrating our
craft to the visitors
and many of them
purchased a variety of
pieces that we had for
sale. Thanks to Lin
for helping take the
pictures.
Allan and Natalia
did double duty at
this year’s festival as
they performed their
music (Cypress
Creek Duo) on the
stage in McBurney
Lane for 45 minutes
at 3:00. Their neighbours came in to
help out at their sales table for that part of the afternoon. Their help was certainly appreciated since
it was a busy time.
All in all the day
was successful
and plans are
already underway for attending the event in
2016.

Betty Scarpino was born in Wenatchee, Washington, USA and earned degree in industrial arts from
the University of Missouri where she also studied
wood sculpture. In her early years she produced
purely functional pieces and that helped her master the techniques that she now uses to create her
sculptural and non-functional pieces. She is now a
full time sculptor, writer, teacher, and printmaker
and has been doing her artistic work for over well a
decade. Her work is featured in museums and private collections in the US and abroad.
Betty was one of our headliners in West Coast
Round-up in 2004 where she endeared herself to us all with her
friendly style, her creativity, and her
willingness to share. It is wonderful to
have her back for a day-long demonstration and a full day hands-on class.
I highly recommend that you take the
time to attend Betty’s demonstration.
Even if you believe that you will never
do work like she does or if you feel you
are “not advanced enough”, you will
gain far more value than the price of
admission. You will also get the
chance to socialize and talk with Betty and other
Guild members during the breaks and at lunch.
So mark your calendar for Saturday, October 24th
and I will see you there.
For more information about Betty and her work
visit her website at www.bettyscarpino.com
Bruce Campbell
October 24th 2015
Upcoming Demonstrator – Betty Scarpino
